paragraphs.text: 3.1 Introduction

runs.text: 3.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: This chapter presents the requirements and designs for the VR text-entry application and user study. It defines the shared interface, six input methods, swipe-recognition workflow, trial management, data collection and descriptive analysis plan. Detailed implementation and empirical results are presented in later chapters.

paragraphs.text: 3.2.1 Functional Requirements

runs.text: 3.2.1 Functional Requirements

paragraphs.text: The application must provide one virtual QWERTY keyboard and support controller ray selection with trigger confirmation, controller ray selection with dwell confirmation, direct controller tapping, controller-based swipe typing, two-index-finger hand-tracked typing and ten-finger hand-tracked typing. It must display the target phrase and current transcription and provide Space, Backspace and Enter controls.

paragraphs.text: The system must provide clear targeting and activation feedback for each method. It must support separate practice and formal trials, a 120-second countdown, participant-ID entry, method selection, phrase progression and trial reset. Swipe typing must capture a continuous gesture, present ranked word candidates and support confirmation or cancellation.

Contact-based methods must prevent repeated activation during continuous contact, and all methods must recover safely from tracking loss or an interrupted trial.

runs.text: 3.3.1 Overall System Architecture

paragraphs.text: Controller and hand-tracking data enter through OpenXR. The trial controller manages phrases, practice/formal state and timing. The data logger produces trial- and sentence-level CSV records. Figure 3.1 summarises this architecture.

paragraphs.text: 3.3.3.1 Trigger-Based Ray Selection

runs.text: 3.3.3.1 Trigger-Based Ray Selection

paragraphs.text: A controller ray targets the keyboard. The intersected key is highlighted, and a small sphere marks the ray-keyboard intersection. Pressing the controller trigger confirms the character.

paragraphs.text: 3.3.3.2 Dwell-Based Ray Selection

runs.text: 3.3.3.2 Dwell-Based Ray Selection

paragraphs.text: This method uses the same ray, key highlight and endpoint marker. A key activates after the ray remains on it for 0.6 seconds. Visual progress indicates the remaining dwell time and resets when the target changes.

paragraphs.text: 3.3.3.3 Direct Controller Tapping

runs.text: 3.3.3.3 Direct Controller Tapping

paragraphs.text: Each controller drives an adjustable virtual stick with a spherical probe. The participant moves the probes to the keyboard and taps keys directly. Separate press and release thresholds prevent repeated activation during continuous contact.

paragraphs.text: 3.3.3.4 Controller-Based Swipe Typing

runs.text: 3.3.3.4 Controller-Based Swipe Typing

paragraphs.text: The participant holds the trigger and moves the ray probe across the letters of a word. Releasing the trigger ends the gesture and opens a list of up to five candidates. The first candidate is highlighted by default; the participant can change the selection, confirm it or cancel the list.

runs.text: 3.3.3.5 Two-Index-Finger Hand-Tracked Typing

paragraphs.text: Only the left and right index fingertips can activate keys. A fingertip contact enters a character, and the fingertip must separate from the key before another activation. Other tracked fingertips remain visible and inactive.

paragraphs.text: 3.3.4 Swipe-Recognition Workflow

runs.text: 3.3.4 Swipe-Recognition Workflow

paragraphs.text: The recogniser projects the controller trajectory onto the keyboard plane, removes redundant or isolated samples, smooths the path and normalises its scale and position. It then generates candidate words from the gesture endpoints and compares the processed path with keyboard-based word templates.

runs.text: The recogniser projects the controller trajectory onto the keyboard plane, removes redundant or isolated samples, smooths the path and normalises its scale and position. It then generates candidate words from the gesture endpoints and compares the processed path with keyboard-based word templates.

paragraphs.text: Candidate ranking combines spatial correspondence, path shape, endpoint distance, movement direction, path length and word frequency. The five highest-ranked words appear in the candidate list. Detailed parameter values and implementation code are presented in the implementation chapter.
